extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, IP policymakers, and attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for determining when information (including internet publications) forms part of the state of the art and how it affects novelty and inventive step, including evidentiary and confidentiality issues. Covers differences for patents vs. utility models and practical rules for office and adversarial proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the state of the art (prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the art comprises all knowledge made available to the public by means of a written or oral description, by use, or in any other way, before the date of priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The German/European formulation is given as the baseline: all information made available to the public by written or oral description, by use or in any other way (see summaries). For utility models (GebrMG/HUMA) the state of the art may be restricted to written descriptions and domestic use. The definition is the fundamental threshold for novelty and inventive step assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of a prior-art disclosure on novelty and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art disclosure that contains all features of an invention destroys novelty; if it makes the invention obvious to the person skilled in the art, it destroys inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the usual tests: novelty = not comprised in a single prior-art item; inventive step = not obvious to the skilled person. Jurisdictional nuances: some systems apply the 'whole contents approach' (e.g., Hungary) so earlier unpublished applications when published can affect novelty but (in certain practices) not inventive step. Also, to avoid double-patenting, content of earlier applications published after a later application's priority date may be treated as prior art for novelty but is typically not considered when examining inventive step (see German/European guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognized means/forms of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure includes written, oral, public use, internet/electronic publications or 'in any other way'. For utility models disclosure may be limited (e.g., written descriptions and domestic use only).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No formal limitation to specific media for patents: electronic and paperless information (internet, online databases, machine-readable media) are generally treated as sufficient disclosure. For utility models, some jurisdictions do not recognize oral or foreign use as prior art. Examiners apply general criteria to determine public accessibility regardless of medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public availability / recipient test
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure is prior art only if members of the public could obtain knowledge of the information and are not bound to keep it confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private communications (private e‑mails) are not prior art simply because technical access might exist. The relevant test is whether the disclosing person made the information available to persons who had no reason to treat it as confidential. Implied confidentiality (e.g., recipients with own commercial secrecy interests) can mean a communication is not public. Conclusive examples and case law are cited (e.g., private dialogs vs. public web pages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality, encryption and password protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Information that is password-protected, encrypted, or otherwise accessible only to a limited, confidentiality‑bound group is not publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the password/decryption tool is only available to a limited/confidential circle, the information is not prior art. A confidentiality obligation can be express or implied (including conclusive implied confidentiality in some circumstances). Jurisdictions provide grace periods if disclosure resulted from an abuse of the applicant's rights or was made by the applicant (e.g., six-month grace in certain laws; WIPO proposals for 12-month applicant grace period are discussed as policy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet-specific indicators (search engines, paywalls, short duration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of a document in a search engine is a strong indicium of public availability but is not strictly necessary; paywalls do not per se prevent public availability if access is available to any person; short-lived but widely read online content can be prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search-engine indexing is an important indicator but not an absolute requirement. Fee-based access should not automatically exclude a publication from the prior art if access by any person is possible. Highly transitory documents (e.g., news items online only for hours) can nonetheless be public if many persons read them. Archives are desirable to establish evidence of publication but are not required to make something prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of disclosure (territorial question)
rubrics_metrics.description: For patents under the European Patent Convention and German Patent Act the place of disclosure is irrelevant; for utility models many laws treat place as relevant, e.g., domestic use only counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under EP/PatG the law does not require determining the geographical place of disclosure. For utility models (GebrMG/HUMA) the place can matter: only written descriptions or uses within the national territory may count. Some national practice (e.g., Hungary) treats internet disclosures as made in every country where the document is accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and duration requirements for electronic disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: There are generally no special formal requirements for the timing or permanence of internet publications beyond the normal rules on priority; the information should be available long enough before the priority date for the public to obtain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except for priority considerations and any statutory novelty grace periods, no extra timing/duration rules are generally imposed. The sufficient duration for an internet posting should be assessed case-by-case; one yardstick is that it must have been available long enough for the public to download or print it. Archives improve evidence but are not required to make a disclosure effective as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and procedures for establishing disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: In ex parte examination the office has a duty to investigate and, where appropriate, to prove a prior-art publication; in adversarial proceedings (oppositions, nullity actions) the party seeking revocation bears the burden of proving that a given prior-art item was published before the relevant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The office follows the principle of official investigation (Amtsermittlungsgrundsatz) in unilateral procedures and the principle of submission/burden of proof (Beibringungsgrundsatz) in two‑party procedures. These principles are applied to internet disclosures as well. The page states this distribution has proven practical and should be retained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary reliability and handling possible manipulation of electronic documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Because digital documents are readily manipulated, doubts about an internet document's authenticity should be considered and corroborating conventional evidence should be sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential manipulation makes it easier to challenge credibility of an internet publication; thus, any doubt about a hardcopy or printout of an internet document should be addressed by additional conventional evidence (e.g., witness testimony, archival records). Nonetheless, the general evidentiary requirements should not differ by publication medium; different grades of evidence for different media are to be rejected because they would impair legal certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understandability to the person skilled in the art (sufficiency of disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art disclosure must be comprehensible to a person skilled in the art without undue burden or inventive experimentation; information obtainable by routine disassembly or reverse engineering counts only if it requires no undue burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the disclosure as the skilled person would have understood it at the priority date. If additional steps (e.g., reverse engineering) are needed, they suffice to constitute disclosure only when they can be carried out without undue burden. Errors in disclosed information should be treated according to how the skilled person would have understood the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of earlier-filed but later-published applications and 'post-published' prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The contents of earlier-filed patent or utility-model applications that are published after the priority/application date of a later application may be taken into account as prior art for novelty in order to avoid double patenting; such post-published prior art is generally not considered when assessing inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several offices consider the contents of earlier-filed applications (published later) as part of the state of the art for novelty between applications covering the same territory, to prevent double patenting. However, that 'post-published' prior art typically is not used in the inventive-step assessment (see German/EP guidance). Jurisdictional rules vary on how these earlier applications are treated for novelty and inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: No need for special new rules for internet disclosures (case-by-case application of existing principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: At present no special statutory rules for internet disclosures are seen as necessary; most questions are factual and can be decided under existing law and case-by-case adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities have found that existing legal frameworks and examination guidelines suffice to handle internet disclosures; courts and offices can resolve the factual issues (public availability, authenticity, timing) using established rules. Nonetheless, international harmonization (e.g., on the definition of state of the art and on novelty grace periods) is recommended as desirable policy.
